claim: Temperature-activated TRP channels (thermoTRPs) are among the only proteins that can directly convert temperature changes into changes in channel open probability.
source: Temperature-activated TRP channels or thermoTRPs are among the only proteins that can directly convert temperature changes into changes in channel open probability.
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of thermoTRPs in the abstract, drawing on established scientific knowledge about these channels.

claim: TRPV1 channels undergo a previously unknown inactivation process that is irreversible.
source: We have carefully characterized the repeated activation of TRPV1 by thermal stimuli and discovered a previously unknown inactivation process, which is irreversible.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The irreversible inactivation in TRPV1 channels is a consequence of the heat absorption process that leads to channel opening.
source: We propose that this form of gating in TRPV1 channels is a consequence of the heat absorption process that leads to channel opening.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' interpretation of their experimental findings.

claim: Thermo TRPs can be activated by changes in temperature alone.
source: Thermo TRPs are unique in that they can be activated by changes in temperature alone (Latorre et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Latorre et al., 2009.

claim: TRPV1 channels respond to temperature increases with a large surge in current produced by both an increment in open probability and single channel-conductance.
source: In particular, TRPV1 channels respond to temperature increases with a large surge in current, produced both by an increment in the open probability and in the single channel-conductance, with the open probability being more temperature dependent.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TRPV1 channel behavior.

claim: The open probability of TRPV1 channels is more temperature dependent than the single channel-conductance.
source: In particular, TRPV1 channels respond to temperature increases with a large surge in current, produced both by an increment in the open probability and in the single channel-conductance, with the open probability being more temperature dependent.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TRPV1 channel behavior.

claim: The mechanism by which absorbed heat is converted into a conformational change triggering TRPV1 channel opening remains largely unknown.
source: The mechanism by which absorbed heat is converted into a conformational change triggering channel opening remains largely unknown (Castillo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: A large positive enthalpy change in the order of tens of kcal·mol−1 is required for TRPV1 activation.
source: A large positive enthalpy change in the order of tens of kcal·mol−1 is required for TRPV1 activation (Yao et al., 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yao et al., 2010a.

claim: The heat dependence of TRPV1 is mostly associated with channel opening while the closing transition is not highly temperature-dependent.
source: This heat dependence is mostly associated with channel opening while the closing transition is not highly temperature-dependent (Yao et al., 2010a; Liu et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yao et al., 2010a and Liu et al., 2003.

claim: Cold-activated channels like TRPM8 show the opposite temperature dependence pattern compared to TRPV1.
source: This is the opposite in cold-activated channels, like TRPM8 (Raddatz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raddatz et al., 2014.

claim: TRPV1 behaves as an allosteric protein.
source: Along with these thermodynamic constrains, TRPV1 behaves as an allosteric protein.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TRPV1.

claim: Allosteric activation of TRPV1 is evidenced by multiple open and closed states.
source: Allosteric activation is evidenced by multiple open and closed states (Liu et al., 2003) and is also observable as a coupling between distinct activation modes when channels are activated by more than one stimulus (Ahern et al., 2005; Jara-Oseguera and Islas, 2013; Brauchi et al., 2004; Jara-Oseguera et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Allosteric activation of TRPV1 is observable as a coupling between distinct activation modes when channels are activated by more than one stimulus.
source: Allosteric activation is evidenced by multiple open and closed states (Liu et al., 2003) and is also observable as a coupling between distinct activation modes when channels are activated by more than one stimulus (Ahern et al., 2005; Jara-Oseguera and Islas, 2013; Brauchi et al., 2004; Jara-Oseguera et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A 'temperature sensor' has not been found in TRPV1 channels.
source: In contrast with the voltage sensor of voltage-gated channels, a 'temperature sensor' has not been found and it has been suggested that temperature might affect several regions of the channel protein at once, explaining why so many regions have been implicated in temperature gating in thermoTRP channels (Cui et al., 2012; Grandl et al., 2008; Yao et al., 2010b; Yao et al., 2011; Brauchi et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Temperature might affect several regions of the TRPV1 channel protein at once.
source: In contrast with the voltage sensor of voltage-gated channels, a 'temperature sensor' has not been found and it has been suggested that temperature might affect several regions of the channel protein at once, explaining why so many regions have been implicated in temperature gating in thermoTRP channels (Cui et al., 2012; Grandl et al., 2008; Yao et al., 2010b; Yao et al., 2011; Brauchi et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many regions have been implicated in temperature gating in thermoTRP channels.
source: In contrast with the voltage sensor of voltage-gated channels, a 'temperature sensor' has not been found and it has been suggested that temperature might affect several regions of the channel protein at once, explaining why so many regions have been implicated in temperature gating in thermoTRP channels (Cui et al., 2012; Grandl et al., 2008; Yao et al., 2010b; Yao et al., 2011; Brauchi et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A possible mechanism for channel gating by temperature invokes a large difference in heat capacity between the closed and open conformations.
source: A possible mechanism for channel gating by temperature invokes a large difference in heat capacity between the closed and open conformations (Clapham and Miller, 2011; Chowdhury et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: One possible way of realizing the heat capacity mechanism is a change in solvation of hydrophobic or hydrophilic regions or residues to a hydrophilic or hydrophobic environment, respectively.
source: One possible way of realizing this mechanism is a change in solvation of hydrophobic or hydrophilic regions or residues to a hydrophilic or hydrophobic environment, respectively.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: TRPV1 activation is coupled to a previously uncharacterized temperature-dependent inactivation process.
source: We find that activation is coupled to a previously uncharacterized temperature-dependent inactivation process and show that this transition is irreversible.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The temperature-dependent inactivation transition in TRPV1 is irreversible.
source: We find that activation is coupled to a previously uncharacterized temperature-dependent inactivation process and show that this transition is irreversible.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The data are suggestive of a partial or complete unfolding of one or more regions of the TRPV1 channel protein during heat absorption.
source: Our data are suggestive of a partial or complete unfolding of one or more regions of the channel protein during heat absorption.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data by the authors.

claim: Temperature ramps used in the study change at a rate of ~15 °C/s.
source: Since these temperature ramps change at a rate of ~15 °C/s and activation of TRPV1 by fast temperature jumps has a time constant in the order of ms (Yao et al., 2009), our ramp measurements can be considered to be in quasi steady-state.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: Activation of TRPV1 by fast temperature jumps has a time constant in the order of milliseconds.
source: Since these temperature ramps change at a rate of ~15 °C/s and activation of TRPV1 by fast temperature jumps has a time constant in the order of ms (Yao et al., 2009), our ramp measurements can be considered to be in quasi steady-state.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yao et al., 2009.

claim: The ramp measurements in the study can be considered to be in quasi steady-state.
source: Since these temperature ramps change at a rate of ~15 °C/s and activation of TRPV1 by fast temperature jumps has a time constant in the order of ms (Yao et al., 2009), our ramp measurements can be considered to be in quasi steady-state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of ramp rate and activation time constant.

claim: Temperature changes in an almost completely symmetrical fashion during the ramps, increasing and decreasing at almost the same rate.
source: Temperature changes in an almost completely symmetrical fashion, increasing and decreasing at almost the same rate.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimulus, observable in Figure 1A.

claim: TRPV1-mediated currents can be activated at both negative and positive potentials.
source: TRPV1-mediated currents can be activated at both negative and positive potentials.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A showing currents at 60 mV and -100 mV.

claim: Channel activity can be observed even at 20°C in multichannel patches.
source: Channel activity can be observed even at 20°C in multichannel patches, and it visibly increases around 40°C (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TRPV1 channel activity visibly increases around 40°C.
source: Channel activity can be observed even at 20°C in multichannel patches, and it visibly increases around 40°C (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TRPV1 current activates and deactivates steeply.
source: Current activates and deactivates steeply, but in spite of the symmetric heat stimulus provided by the ramp, the current response is not symmetrical (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Despite the symmetric heat stimulus provided by the ramp, the TRPV1 current response is not symmetrical.
source: Current activates and deactivates steeply, but in spite of the symmetric heat stimulus provided by the ramp, the current response is not symmetrical (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The current during temperature decrease is less steep than the up-ramp current.
source: It is apparent that the current during temperature decrease is less steep than the up-ramp current, so current activation-deactivation is accompanied by a high degree of hysteresis.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1D.

claim: TRPV1 current activation-deactivation is accompanied by a high degree of hysteresis.
source: It is apparent that the current during temperature decrease is less steep than the up-ramp current, so current activation-deactivation is accompanied by a high degree of hysteresis.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1D and is an inference from the asymmetric current response.

claim: Hysteresis in TRPV1 activation is not a consequence of the speed of the ramp.
source: Hysteresis is not a consequence of the speed of the ramp, since a slower ramp (7 °C/s) produces the same result.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different ramp speeds.

claim: Activation by slower ramps proceeds with a high enthalpy, not significantly different from activation by the faster ramp.
source: Also, activation by slower ramps proceeds with a high enthalpy, not significantly different from activation by the faster ramp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The magnitude of the TRPV1 temperature-activated current is reduced with each subsequent ramp.
source: A key novel observation is that the magnitude of the TRPV1 temperature-activated current is reduced with each subsequent ramp.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After several activation episodes, TRPV1 currents almost completely disappear.
source: Strikingly, after several activation episodes, currents almost completely disappear (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The reduction of TRPV1 current becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures.
source: The reduction of current becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different temperatures.

claim: When the ramp reaches temperatures near 55°C, current decay is visible even before the ramp gets to its maximum temperature.
source: When the ramp reaches temperatures near 55°C, current decay is visible even before the ramp gets to its maximum temperature (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The decay of TRPV1 current as a function of time is temperature-dependent.
source: The decay of current as a function of time is temperature-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Current loss when activating by ramps that reach moderate temperatures (41–43°C) proceeds more slowly than when channels are activated by ramps above 50°C.
source: Current loss when activating by ramps that reach moderate temperatures (41–43°C) proceeds more slowly than when channels are activated by ramps above 50°C (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Current loss upon heating occurs when the patch is held at a negative voltage of −60 mV.
source: Current loss upon heating also occurs when the patch is held at a negative voltage of −60 mV (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Activation of TRPV1 is more steeply dependent on temperature at negative voltages.
source: Activation of TRPV1 is more steeply dependent on temperature at negative voltages, which is reflected in the enthalpy of activation being significantly higher at −60 mV than at 60 mV (Figure 2E), as expected from its allosteric coupling (Jara-Oseguera et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and is consistent with allosteric coupling cited from Jara-Oseguera et al., 2016.

claim: The enthalpy of activation is significantly higher at −60 mV than at 60 mV.
source: Activation of TRPV1 is more steeply dependent on temperature at negative voltages, which is reflected in the enthalpy of activation being significantly higher at −60 mV than at 60 mV (Figure 2E), as expected from its allosteric coupling (Jara-Oseguera et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Current loss at negative voltage proceeds faster than at positive voltages for the same temperature.
source: Concurrently, current loss at negative voltage proceeds faster than at positive voltages for the same temperature (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Current loss is not caused by patch excision.
source: Current loss is not caused by patch excision, since it can be observed in whole-cell and outside-out recordings, with similar characteristics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 comparing different recording configurations.

claim: The mechanism of current loss is a property of the TRPV1 polypeptide and is not caused by the loss of a stabilizing factor upon patch excision.
source: This suggests that the mechanism of current loss is a property of the TRPV1 polypeptide and is not caused by the loss of a stabilizing factor upon patch excision, as described for other TRP channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that current loss occurs in multiple recording configurations.

claim: In a previous study, it was observed that TRPV1 activation after challenging the channel with two high temperature pulses was stable.
source: In a previous study (Liu and Qin, 2016), it was observed that TRPV1 activation, after challenging the channel with two high temperature pulses was stable.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study by Liu and Qin, 2016.

claim: Inactivation is observed when a series, more than two, of high temperature pulses are applied.
source: The present study shows that inactivation is observed when a series, more than two, of high temperature pulses are applied.
evidence: This is a finding of the present study that extends previous observations.

claim: The reduction of current amplitude resulting from repetitive stimulation is accompanied by a dramatic change in the sensitivity of channels to temperature.
source: An important observation is the fact that the reduction of current amplitude resulting from repetitive stimulation is accompanied by a dramatic change in the sensitivity of channels to temperature.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Temperature sensitivity of TRPV1 is mainly determined by the apparent activation ΔH.
source: This sensitivity is mainly determined by the apparent activation ΔH.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about temperature sensitivity.

claim: The response of TRPV1 to the first ramp results in a very steep activation curve.
source: The response of TRPV1 to the first ramp results in a very steep activation curve.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Subsequent activation curves show reduced slopes, indicating a reduction of the ΔH associated with opening.
source: Subsequent activation curves show reduced slopes, indicating a reduction of the ΔH associated with opening.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: After five ramps reaching a maximum temperature of 48.7°C, the ΔH of activation is reduced to near 10 kcal⋅mol−1.
source: After five ramps, reaching a maximum temperature of 48.7°C, the ΔH of activation is reduced to near 10 kcal⋅mol−1, or a Q10 value of 1–2, which is similar to diffusion processes (Sidell and Hazel, 1987) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A Q10 value of 1–2 is similar to diffusion processes.
source: After five ramps, reaching a maximum temperature of 48.7°C, the ΔH of activation is reduced to near 10 kcal⋅mol−1, or a Q10 value of 1–2, which is similar to diffusion processes (Sidell and Hazel, 1987) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sidell and Hazel, 1987.

claim: TRPV1 current could not be elicited after a recovery period following inactivation by more than 50%.
source: Surprisingly, current could not be elicited after the recovery period.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lack of recovery is observed when current is inactivated by application of several ramps at moderate temperature.
source: Lack of recovery is observed when current is inactivated by application of several ramps at moderate temperature (Figure 3A and C) or during a single ramp at high temperature (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, C, D, and F.

claim: Lack of recovery is observed when current is inactivated during a single ramp at high temperature.
source: Lack of recovery is observed when current is inactivated by application of several ramps at moderate temperature (Figure 3A and C) or during a single ramp at high temperature (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, C, D, and F.

claim: Current loss is irreversible even if the temperature was lowered to ~10°C during the recovery period.
source: Again, current loss was irreversible even if the temperature was lowered to ~10°C during the recovery period (Figure 3B,C,E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C, E, and F.

claim: Extending the recovery period from 2 to 20 min failed to produce any recuperation of current.
source: Finally, extending the recovery period from 2 to 20 min failed to produce any recuperation of current, regardless of the membrane potential value during recovery (0 or −60 mV, Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G–I.

claim: Presence of intracellular ATP interferes with calcium-induced desensitization, presumably due to occlusion of calcium-calmodulin binding at the N-terminal domain.
source: Presence of intracellular ATP interferes with calcium-induced desensitization, presumably due to occlusion of calcium-calmodulin binding at the N-terminal domain (Lishko et al., 2007; Rosenbaum et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lishko et al., 2007 and Rosenbaum et al., 2004.

claim: 10 mM ATP applied to the inside of patches had no effect on temperature activation of TRPV1.
source: 10 mM ATP applied to the inside of patches had no effect on temperature activation and more importantly, on inactivation induced by repetitive activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 10 mM ATP applied to the inside of patches had no effect on inactivation induced by repetitive activation.
source: 10 mM ATP applied to the inside of patches had no effect on temperature activation and more importantly, on inactivation induced by repetitive activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation by capsaicin is impaired after multiple temperature ramps.
source: Surprisingly, activation by capsaicin is also impaired after multiple temperature ramps (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Capsaicin elicits robust TRPV1 currents.
source: Capsaicin elicits robust currents, but the response to a second application after several activating ramps, is highly diminished (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The response to a second application of capsaicin after several activating ramps is highly diminished.
source: Capsaicin elicits robust currents, but the response to a second application after several activating ramps, is highly diminished (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a clear inverse correlation between the extent of current loss induced by temperature and the magnitude of current activated by the second application of capsaicin.
source: There is a clear inverse correlation between the extent of current loss induced by temperature and the magnitude of current activated by the second application of capsaicin (Figure 4B), suggesting that the remaining capsaicin-sensitive channels have not yet undergone inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The remaining capsaicin-sensitive channels have not yet undergone inactivation.
source: There is a clear inverse correlation between the extent of current loss induced by temperature and the magnitude of current activated by the second application of capsaicin (Figure 4B), suggesting that the remaining capsaicin-sensitive channels have not yet undergone inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inverse correlation observed.

claim: Application of the temperature ramp in the presence of capsaicin produced an increase in current.
source: Application of the temperature ramp in the presence of capsaicin, produced an increase in current, as expected (Figure 4C), which had a reduced slope, since the channels are being activated by capsaicin and heat at the same time (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The current increase in the presence of capsaicin had a reduced slope since the channels are being activated by capsaicin and heat at the same time.
source: Application of the temperature ramp in the presence of capsaicin, produced an increase in current, as expected (Figure 4C), which had a reduced slope, since the channels are being activated by capsaicin and heat at the same time (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed reduced slope, supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: The channels entered the temperature-induced inactivated state regardless of the continued presence of capsaicin.
source: Remarkably, the channels entered the temperature-induced inactivated state regardless of the continued presence of capsaicin and the current was reduced to leak levels.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Several regions in TRPV1 channels, including the N-terminal ankyrin domains, the transmembrane domains, the pore region and the C-terminus, have been implicated in temperature gating.
source: Several regions in TRPV1 channels, including the N-terminal ankyrin domains, the transmembrane domains, the pore region and the C-terminus, have been implicated in temperature gating (Cui et al., 2012; Grandl et al., 2008; Yao et al., 2011; Laursen et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2010; Grandl et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The apparently distributed heat sensitivity suggests that several regions contribute discretely to heat absorption or its coupling to channel opening.
source: This apparently distributed heat sensitivity suggests that several regions contribute discretely to heat absorption or its coupling to channel opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple regions are implicated in temperature gating.

claim: Inactivation proceeds with a time course in the order of tens of seconds.
source: Inactivation proceeds with a time course in the order of tens of seconds.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: The time course of inactivation is strongly dependent on the maximum temperature attained during the activation ramp.
source: The time course is strongly dependent on the maximum temperature attained during the activation ramp, behaving as if inactivation was coupled to opening.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Temperature-dependent inactivation in TRPV1 resembles open state inactivation in voltage-dependent channels.
source: In this regard, temperature-dependent inactivation in TRPV1 resembles open state inactivation in voltage-dependent channels (Demo and Yellen, 1991; Aldrich et al., 1983).
evidence: This is a comparison supported by citations to Demo and Yellen, 1991 and Aldrich et al., 1983.

claim: TRPV1 inactivation is irreversible, unlike open state inactivation in voltage-dependent channels.
source: In this regard, temperature-dependent inactivation in TRPV1 resembles open state inactivation in voltage-dependent channels (Demo and Yellen, 1991; Aldrich et al., 1983). However TRPV1 inactivation is irreversible.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study distinguishing TRPV1 from voltage-dependent channels.

claim: Heat might be absorbed in several regions of the TRPV1 channel, leading to partial contributions to channel opening.
source: Heat might be absorbed in several regions of the channel, leading to partial contributions to channel opening, but some regions might absorb heat through a mechanism akin to partial polypeptide denaturation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Some regions of TRPV1 might absorb heat through a mechanism akin to partial polypeptide denaturation.
source: Heat might be absorbed in several regions of the channel, leading to partial contributions to channel opening, but some regions might absorb heat through a mechanism akin to partial polypeptide denaturation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Channels undergoing partial denaturation would become less able to absorb or convert heat into a conformational change, resulting in reduced apparent enthalpy of activation.
source: Channels undergoing this partial denaturation would become less able to absorb or convert heat into a conformational change, resulting in reduced apparent enthalpy of activation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors to explain their observations.

claim: After opening, channels become sufficiently distorted and enter the inactivated state irreversibly.
source: Finally, after opening, channels become sufficiently distorted and enter the inactivated state irreversibly.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: The proposed mechanism is consistent with the high heat capacity change (∆Cp) mechanism.
source: This is consistent with the high heat capacity change (∆Cp) mechanism (Clapham and Miller, 2011; Chowdhury et al., 2014) and might reflect alterations of hydrophobic interactions through solvent exposure (Sosa-Pagán et al., 2017) and not large conformational changes (De-la-Rosa et al., 2013; Ruigrok et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the findings to existing theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: The mechanism might reflect alterations of hydrophobic interactions through solvent exposure and not large conformational changes.
source: This is consistent with the high heat capacity change (∆Cp) mechanism (Clapham and Miller, 2011; Chowdhury et al., 2014) and might reflect alterations of hydrophobic interactions through solvent exposure (Sosa-Pagán et al., 2017) and not large conformational changes (De-la-Rosa et al., 2013; Ruigrok et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: HEK293 cells were used for the experiments.
source: We used the HEK293 cell line obtained from ATCC 10 years ago, cell identity has not been authenticated, but we have tested for mycoplasma and the cells are free of infection.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: The HEK293 cell line was obtained from ATCC 10 years ago.
source: We used the HEK293 cell line obtained from ATCC 10 years ago, cell identity has not been authenticated, but we have tested for mycoplasma and the cells are free of infection.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: The HEK293 cells are free of mycoplasma infection.
source: We used the HEK293 cell line obtained from ATCC 10 years ago, cell identity has not been authenticated, but we have tested for mycoplasma and the cells are free of infection.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials and quality control.

claim: Electrophysiological experiments were carried out on rat TRPV1-WT cloned in the plasmid pcDNA3.
source: Electrophysiological experiments were carried out on rat TRPV1-WT cloned in the plasmid pcDNA3.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: Patch clamp recordings were made from HEK293 cells expressing TRPV1 in the inside-out, whole-cell and outside-out configurations.
source: Patch clamp recordings were made from HEK293 cells expressing TRPV1 in the inside-out, whole-cell and outside-out configurations of the patch-clamp recording technique.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Temperature activation was carried out using a micro-heater that uses the resistive heating principle.
source: Temperature activation was carried out using a micro-heater that uses the resistive heating principle as previously described (Islas et al., 2015), with the modification that, in this study, we used a programmable current-regulated DC power supply (Agilent) controlled via a Python program.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with a citation to a previous description.

claim: The pipette with seal was placed approximately 27 µm from the micro-heater for all recordings and temperature calibrations.
source: For all recordings and temperature calibrations, the pipette with seal was placed approximately 27 µm from the micro-heater, in the case of whole-cell recording the cell was lifted and placed in front of the micro-heater.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The membrane potential was held constant at the indicated potential, typically 60 mV, during temperature ramp application.
source: The membrane potential was held constant at the indicated potential, typically 60 mV, during temperature ramp application.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.
